newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 28.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 28.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- POWER CHIEF 'NATURAL CHOICE' FOR AMERICANS

Norman Askew, the chief executive of UK regional electricity company East Midlands Electricity (EME), has been appointed president and chief executive officer of Virginia Power, the US utility which is the main subsidiary of EME's new American owner, Dominion Resources. Askew will be the first British boss of an American electricity company.
-- HK SCARE LEADS ROLLS TO MODIFY ENGINES

Engine maker Rolls Royce is to make changes to its Trent 700 series after failures that forced two Hong Kong airlines to ground 15 aircraft for three days. The problem also resulted in three emergency landings by the aircraft -- Airbus two-engined A330-300 -- which are owned by the Cathay Pacific group. Rolls Royce says its engineers have now pin-pointed the reason for the problem, which centred on poor oil lubrication of a bearing in a French-made gearbox.
-- TALK OF SPECIAL DIVIDEND LIFTS BOOTS

Shares in retailer Boots rose 12p to 725p on Tuesday on speculation that the group intends to return 400 million stg cash to its shareholders. While a spokesman for the company declined to confirm that a special dividend is planned, Boots is due to report its annual results next week and analysts believe that an announcement may be made.
THE TIMES
-- AT&T PLANS RECORD $55 BILLION MERGER WITH SBC

US telecoms company AT&T is planning a $55 billion mega merger with SBC, the leading US regional phone operator. The deal would be the largest merger in history, and would reshape the global telecommunications market. The new company would have about $80 billion in annual revenue, and would be the world's largest phone company.
-- EU CLOSE TO DEAL WITH US ON LICENSING OF NEW DRUGS

The European Union is reported to be close to signing the Mutual Recognition Agreement, a deal with the US that would make it easier for pharmaceutical companies to secure regulatory licences for their products. Completion of the agreement would represent a boost to UK drugs companies as it would slash the time spent on clinical tests of drugs and other medical products both in the US and Europe.
-- TAYLOR WARNS ON EMU

Martin Taylor, chief executive of Barclays, has called on currency speculators to 'blow apart' any too hasty move to a common currency. Speaking in Switzerland, Taylor -- recently appointed head of the government's task force to reform the tax and benefits system -- cited recent problems in France and Germany to claim there is now a much lower chance of Emu starting on time.
THE GUARDIAN
-- TOBACCO BAN IS URGED ON CO-OP

The managing director of the Co-operative Bank, Terry Thomas, has called on retailers to stop selling cigarettes. The plea came as Thomas, who has been credited with reviving the bank's fortunes by promoting an ethical stance, received an award for the bank's advertising campaign against the sale of landmines.
-- GOLDMAN SACHS REJECTS TAX RISE FEARS

Gavyn Davies, chief economist at investment bank Goldman Sachs, has claimed that calls from business leaders for Chancellor Gordon Brown to raise taxes in his summer budget are based on overblown and inaccurate fears of a 'black hole' in public finances. The comments were made as Davies -- who has been tipped as a future governor of the Bank of England -- unveiled the Green Budget, an annual collaboration between Goldman Sachs and the Institute for Fiscal Studies.
-- JOSPIN VETOES TELECOM SELL-OFF

The leader of the French socialist party, Lionel Jospin, has warned that he may derail the privatisation of France Telecom should his party win the second round of voting in the French elections this weekend. The sale of France Telecom, which had been put in motion by the outgoing centre-right government, had been expected to raise up to FFr50 billion (5.5 billion stg) and would be the country's largest privatisation to date.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- SCHRODER VENTURES LAUNCHES $1 BILLION PRIVATE EQUITY FUND

In a bid to attract American institutions into the European venture capital market, Schroder Ventures has launched Europe's first ever $1 billion private equity fund. North America provided 50 percent of the money for the venture, which aims to cash in on a wave of corporate and industrial restructuring sweeping through continental Europe.
-- RESEARCH SPENDING SOARS AT CAMBRIDGE

Cambridge Antibody Trust, the company formed from a spin-off from the Medical Research Council, has reported a sharp rise in research and development spending with its maiden results. The company registered a rise in pre-tax losses from 580,000 stg to 6.7 million stg for the six months to March 31. Cambridge said it was on target to complete trials on an antibody for eye fibrosis by the end of 1997.
-- GREMLIN SETS OUT ITS STALL TO DOUBLE PROFITS

Computer and video games software company Gremlin Interactive, which plans a stock market listing in London in July, has said it is aiming to double its profits within two years of coming to market. The company is expected to be valued at between 45 million stg and 55 million stg, and intends to use the proceeds of the float to fund an increase in the number of games it releases each year from six to around 15.
